projects.name: WeVibe
projects.subtitle: A landscape-photo feed where the sessions and the threads hold
projects.description: A social platform for landscape photography built end to end — feed, likes, two-level threaded replies, profiles, JWT sessions and image uploads kept out of the records.
projects.role: Solo — data model, auth, interface, deployment

sections.overview:
A feed of landscape photography with the parts a feed needs to be more than a list: accounts that
survive a reload, comments that nest under other comments, likes that persist, and uploads that stay
out of the database row.
sections.problem:
The versions I kept finding stopped at the feed. The interesting work — a reply that belongs to a
comment rather than to a post, a session that lasts, an image stored somewhere other than the
document that references it — was the part nobody showed done properly.
sections.solution:
Posts, comments and replies are separate Mongoose collections with parent references, so one thread
renders from a single query instead of a chain of them. Sessions are JWTs signed with `jose`;
passwords are hashed with bcrypt; the verification mail goes through Nodemailer. Images upload to
ImageKit and the document keeps only the URL. Reads go through server components, mutations through
server actions, and every mutation route re-reads the session from the cookie rather than trusting
what the client sent.
sections.features:
- Infinite feed in batches of eight, with a shuffled deck that does not repeat what is on screen
- Likes, and comments with one level of replies under them
- Profiles with posts, a with-media tab, followers and following lists
- Meet people: every account ordered by followers, each one followable in place
- Search by username, profile editing, email and password change, account deletion behind a
  password confirmation
- Verified badges granted by the site, never chosen by the account
- Loading states that show the shape of what is arriving instead of a button that changes its mind
sections.architecture:
Next.js app router on Vercel, MongoDB (Atlas) with Mongoose documents for users, posts, comments and
replies. Public catalogue pages use time-based revalidation so repeat visits do not touch the
database. The interface is one stylesheet of design tokens plus Tailwind utilities, with a bottom
tab bar under 640px and a left rail above it. Sessions are cookies: fourteen days with Remember me,
one hour without.
sections.challenges:
The first thread model needed one query per comment and fell over on long threads; replies moved
into their own collection. Feed paging flickered because the scroll observer was rebuilt on every
loading flip and re-fired for a strip already on screen — the guard now lives in a ref, and the
observer is rebuilt only when the tab changes. Controls that depend on who is signed in pulse while
the session is being read, so a Follow button never paints on your own profile and flips a beat
later.
sections.results:
Live on Vercel with a working feed, likes, threaded replies, editable profiles and account deletion.
Built and maintained by one person across the data model, the auth, the upload pipeline and the
interface.
sections.future:
Two levels of reply is a deliberate limit; deeper nesting is not planned until there is a reason for
it.

projects.name: Signal Field — Issue 01
projects.subtitle: An online CV laid out as a magazine issue, with a field that re-forms as you scroll
projects.description: The interactive portfolio and online CV of Alexandru Saraev: seven art-directed plates, one procedural 3D field, case studies as real pages, and a project list that fills itself from PORTFOLIO.md files in GitHub repositories.
projects.role: Solo — art direction, interface, 3D layer, data pipeline, static build

sections.overview:
A CV that reads as an issue of a magazine rather than as a form: a cover, seven plates, and a
procedural field of bars, dust and a sculptural band that responds to how far you have read. It is
a static export — `next build` writes `out/` and any static host serves it.
sections.problem:
Most online CVs are a list of jobs beside a list of technologies. The interesting question — what
kind of builder am I — is answered by how the page is made, not by the bullet points on it. And a
project list that has to be edited by hand goes stale the week after it is written.
sections.solution:
Content and presentation are separated in three places. `lib/site.ts` holds the copy, roles, skills
and contact details. `lib/curated.ts` holds the hand-written case studies. And any repository that
carries a `PORTFOLIO.md` in its root is picked up by `tools/sync.ts`, validated against the schema in
`lib/portfolio.ts`, measured for its real image sizes and merged into `content/projects.json` — one
`Case` model, so the same renderer designs a curated plate entry and a GitHub-driven one. No
component edits are needed to publish a project.
sections.features:
- Seven plates: cover, approach, capabilities, work, process, CV, contact
- A WebGL field built from instanced bars, signal dust and a sculptural band, driven by scroll
  progress rather than by a fixed timeline
- Case studies as prerendered pages, each with its own title and description
- A GitHub Actions workflow that regenerates the project feed every six hours and proves the site
  still builds from it
- A documented `PORTFOLIO.md` schema — Zod-validated, with the parser under test
- Reduced-motion and no-JavaScript paths that show the same content
sections.architecture:
Next.js App Router with `output: 'export'`, so there is no server, no API routes and no database —
which is also why no GitHub credential can reach the browser. Three.js comes in through
@react-three/fiber; `lib/field/state.ts` is the only meeting point between the DOM layer and WebGL.
Plain CSS with tokens for palette, type scale, spacing and motion; no UI library.
sections.challenges:
Scroll choreography over a WebGL canvas: the reveals, the folio rail and the field all needed one
source of scroll truth, and passing numbers through React state re-rendered the page on every frame.
The `PORTFOLIO.md` gate is deliberately narrow — the file's presence in a repository root is the
only thing that decides whether a project appears — because every wider rule turned into metadata
that had to be maintained by hand.
sections.results:
Served as a static site from GitHub Pages, with the project feed regenerated on a schedule and the
schema itself under test.
sections.future:
The feed currently reads one GitHub account. A second source — local projects with no repository —
is not planned until there is a reason for it.
